Juniper Travel: AI Governance Overview

Governance
We prefer to work with reputable vendors. Teams are encouraged to think about possible impacts of their AI. We have a spreadsheet of some of the AI tools teams told us about. Optional lunch-and-learn sessions on AI are sometimes offered. Teams are generally expected to take responsibility for the AI they use. We aim to stay aware of new AI regulation as it develops. People are expected to use their judgement when relying on AI output.

Mapping and context
Before development, the product owner documents the use case, target users, deployment setting and out-of-scope uses in a one-page brief. Documentation for each system describes where it performs poorly and tells operators when they must check results manually. Supervisors keep an eye on how the AI is working. We try to use well-known open source models.

Measurement and testing
Models are tested before they go live. We use machine learning to improve search ranking and product recommendations. People can contact customer service with any concerns. We track defined metrics for accuracy, robustness and harm for each system, and the risks we cannot yet measure are listed in the risk register.

Management and response
Serious problems would be escalated to management. The annual report is published each spring and covers financial performance. A post-deployment monitoring plan is required for each system, covering user feedback capture, appeal and override, change management and decommissioning. Technology is central to how we serve our customers. We could turn the system off if we had to. The data science team is based in two offices and works in two-week sprints. Our values are integrity, curiosity and respect for people. The marketing team uses AI tools to draft campaign ideas. We are committed to ethical business practices across the organisation.

Kestrel Motors: AI Governance Overview

Governance
Vendors supplying AI components must pass a security and AI-risk assessment, and contracts include clauses on data use, intellectual property and audit rights. All staff who build or approve AI complete the annual AI risk training, and completion is tracked by HR. Each AI system has a named business owner and a named technical owner, and escalation paths are written in the governance handbook. The marketing team uses AI tools to draft campaign ideas. Before any AI project starts, counsel confirms which statutory duties apply and records the answer in the project file. The oversight standard states which decisions need human approval, which need human review afterwards, and who performs each. Teams are encouraged to think about possible impacts of their AI.

Mapping and context
The architecture review lists third-party AI components and assesses legal, copyright and supply-chain risk for each. Each AI system has a charter that states its intended purpose, the users and context of use, and the laws that apply to it. We use machine learning to improve search ranking and product recommendations. Oversight workflows are written for every high-risk system, with assigned reviewers and sign-off steps. Product launches follow a quarterly release calendar. Employees can use the internal wiki to find team documentation. Our values are integrity, curiosity and respect for people.

Measurement and testing
Before release, each model is validated on held-out data and the results, including how far they generalise, are documented. Customers and staff can report problems with AI decisions through a dedicated form and can appeal outcomes to a human reviewer, and reports feed our evaluation metrics. We track defined metrics for accuracy, robustness and harm for each system, and the risks we cannot yet measure are listed in the risk register. Security reviews cover model theft, data poisoning and prompt injection, and resilience tests are documented. The company was founded in 2009 and now operates in eleven countries. Privacy risks, including re-identification and data leakage, are examined and recorded before deployment. Each model is tested for performance differences across demographic groups and the results and mitigations are documented. Live system behaviour is tracked continuously against baseline performance, with thresholds that trigger investigation. Colleagues sometimes look over each other's work.

Management and response
AI incidents are logged and reported to the governance committee within 72 hours, and affected users are notified according to the incident response policy. Runbooks describe how to deactivate or replace a model quickly, and the procedure is tested each year. The data science team is based in two offices and works in two-week sprints. Residual risks are documented in the release notes and accepted in writing by the business owner. Each release includes a plan for ongoing monitoring, incident response, updates and eventual retirement of the model. We are committed to ethical business practices across the organisation.

Brightpath Bank: AI Governance Overview

Governance
The Legal & Compliance team maintains a register of laws and regulations that apply to our AI use, including the EU AI Act and GDPR, and reviews it every quarter. The Chief Data Officer is accountable for AI risk; model owners, reviewers and approvers are named in a RACI chart published on the intranet. The oversight standard states which decisions need human approval, which need human review afterwards, and who performs each. New hires in data and product roles take a mandatory AI ethics and risk course within 60 days, and contractors take it too. The marketing team uses AI tools to draft campaign ideas. We prefer to work with reputable vendors. Product launches follow a quarterly release calendar. IT keeps a living catalogue of all models and AI-enabled tools, and unregistered systems may not be deployed. Project teams complete an AI impact assessment for each new system, recording potential harms to individuals and society, and file it with the governance office.

Mapping and context
Each deployed system has a defined oversight procedure naming who monitors outputs, how often, and what they do when something looks wrong. Each AI system has a charter that states its intended purpose, the users and context of use, and the laws that apply to it. Model cards list known limitations, failure modes and unsupported inputs, and state how staff should interpret and verify outputs. Risk assessments rate the likelihood and severity of each identified benefit and harm on a 5-point scale and are reviewed by the risk committee. For every external model, library or dataset we use, a component review records its licence, provenance and legal and security risks.

Measurement and testing
Technology is central to how we serve our customers. The company was founded in 2009 and now operates in eleven countries. Production models are monitored with dashboards for drift, error rates and unusual outputs, and alerts go to the on-call owner. We are proud of our culture of innovation and customer focus. We comply with GDPR in general. An appeals process lets affected people challenge AI-driven decisions, and complaint data is reviewed monthly. A measurement plan names the metrics, test methods and thresholds for each AI risk, with gaps recorded. Security reviews cover model theft, data poisoning and prompt injection, and resilience tests are documented. An external auditor reviews our high-risk systems every year. Before release, each model is validated on held-out data and the results, including how far they generalise, are documented. We are committed to ethical business practices across the organisation. Bias and fairness evaluations are run before release and every six months, using defined fairness metrics.

Management and response
Every AI system has a documented kill switch and rollback procedure, and an owner is authorised to disable it if it behaves outside its intended use. Serious problems would be escalated to management. We intend to keep an eye on systems after launch. The annual report is published each spring and covers financial performance. Employees can use the internal wiki to find team documentation.

Cobalt Logistics: AI Governance Overview

Governance
An inventory of AI systems is planned for next year. Teams must write up foreseeable risks and impacts of every AI system in a standard template that is reviewed by the risk function. Our supplier policy requires disclosure of models, data sources and subcontractors for any AI product, and the clauses are reviewed by legal. Responsibilities for AI oversight are assigned in writing, from the board risk committee down to individual model stewards. Role-based AI risk training is delivered each year, with advanced modules for model developers and reviewers. Applicable legal obligations for AI are tracked in a compliance matrix owned by the General Counsel and updated whenever the law changes.

Mapping and context
Our sustainability programme aims to reduce office energy use by 20 percent. Formal oversight procedures are under discussion.

Measurement and testing
We will look at AI-specific attacks later. A validation report shows the model performs consistently on representative data and notes where results may not transfer. Automated monitoring compares deployed model outputs with expected behaviour and logs deviations daily. Fairness testing is on the roadmap. We may ask an outside expert to review important systems in future. Our customer support team is available around the clock in six languages. Metrics will be chosen once the system is more mature.

Management and response
Significant AI failures are communicated to the relevant teams and customers, and the response is tracked until closure. The board meets four times a year. We value responsible and trustworthy AI as part of our mission. Teams handle updates as they see fit. Cloud infrastructure is provided under a multi-year contract with a major provider. A shutdown procedure is being considered.

The security team assesses each AI system for attacks and failure resilience before go-live and annually after. Privacy is considered where personal data is obviously involved. If a system drifts outside its approved scope, the owner can suspend it immediately under the deactivation policy. Remaining risks are discussed informally.
